unverified: That Gordon Foster wrote a 1966 report for W. H. Smith. Both official agency histories describe the SBN's creation without naming any individual: R. R. Bowker's isbn.org says W. H. Smith 'hired consultants' and that 'They devised the Standard Book Numbering (SBN) system in 1966', and the International ISBN Agency's Users' Manual credits 'J. Whitaker & Sons, Ltd.' The Wikipedia claim carries a 'citation needed' tag. What is confirmed is the Library of Congress record for F. G. Foster, 'Standard numbering in the book trade', Publishers Association, London, 1967, 9 p. The prose claims only that.
The text of Foster's report. Only the Library of Congress catalogue record was opened, not the nine pages themselves; no quotation from the report appears in the prose.

That Foster's report is the document that fixed the nine-digit width. The Library of Congress record attests the report's author, publisher, date and nine-page length; ISO Focus+ separately attests that a nine-digit scheme with a final validation character 'quickly gained acceptance from 1967'. The prose states the two facts as two sentences and does not join them causally.

The personal roles of David Whitaker and Emery Koltay. The Users' Manual names the firms — J. Whitaker & Sons, Ltd. (UK, 1967) and R. R. Bowker (US, 1968) — not the individuals. Neither name appears in the prose.

That the English-language registration groups specifically were exhausted by 2005, and that variable-length block hoarding and mis-sizing rather than title volume consumed the 10-digit space. The ISO news item attributes the pressure to 'the very success of the ISBN system' and to 'the explosive growth of electronic publishing', and names no registration group. The prose makes no group-level or cause-attribution claim.
Any figure for what the ISBN-13 migration cost the book trade. The only currency figure found and used is the 99 Swiss franc list price of ISO 2108:2005, stated on the ISO news page.
That ISBN-10 and ISBN-13 still coexist in library and retail databases today. Not claimed in the prose.

Date conflict, recorded and avoided: the International ISBN Agency's own ISQ article 'ISBN: A History' (Stella Griffiths, ISQ vol. 27 no. 2&3, 2015) dates ISO's first publication of ISBN to 1972, while the same agency's Users' Manual (7th ed.) and its ISO Focus+ article both say 1970. No bare ISO-approval year appears in the prose.
